abstract.p: Natural components, evolved to help organisms adapt and defend against threats, are also vital sources for drug discovery due to their diverse and potent bioactivities. In the present work, we proposed the Gene-encoded Natural Diverse Components Repository (GNDC, https://cbcb.cdutcm.edu.cn/gndc/), a primary and most extensive database dedicated to cataloging diverse natural components. GNDC currently catalogs over 234 million natural components that are organized into four specialized sub-databases: HerbalMDB for 2.32 million secondary metabolites, HerbalPDB for 229 million small peptides, HerbalRDB for 2.38 million small RNAs, and HerbalCDB for 0.26 million carbohydrates. By leveraging customized pipelines for high-throughput multi-omics data and AI technologies, the GNDC enables large-scale discovery and annotation of natural products from nuclear and organellar genomes of species listed in eight global pharmacopoeias and multi-resource data. Compared to existing resources, GNDC achieves a 10-fold increase in component yield and introduces over 200 million previously unreported components. To support this unprecedented data volume and complexity, state-of-the-art AI tools are seamlessly integrated to decipher and annotate vast data collections, such as classification and gene expression signature generation of millions of secondary metabolites. We envision that the GNDC will drive the transformation of drug discovery from an “experience-driven” approach to a “big data-driven” paradigm.

list-item.p: GNDC is the world’s primary and most extensive database focused on gene-encoded diverse natural components.
GNDC presently comprises over 234 million natural components categorized into four distinct sub-databases.
Custom pipelines and AI tools boost component yield and facilitate in-depth analysis.
The vast chemical space of GNDC enhances the big data-driven paradigm for drug discovery.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Natural components are the evolutionary products of organisms.1 They are not only essential for sustaining fundamental physiological functions of organisms but also serve as key mediators in adaptation, competition, and defense against environmental challenges.2,3,4 Due to their potent pharmacological activities, natural components have also been extensively explored as foundational resources for drug discovery.5,6 Their diverse bioactivities have led to the identification of numerous natural components that serve as the basis for many pharmaceutical agents.7

Despite their importance, conventional classifications of natural components have primarily focused on secondary metabolites,8 often overlooking gene-encoded molecules such as small RNA (sRNA) and peptides. This limitation highlights the need for a more comprehensive and integrative classification system that incorporates genomic insights alongside the chemical and functional information of natural components.

To address this gap, we propose a novel classification system for natural components grounded in the central dogma of molecular biology. Based on this framework (Figures 1 and S1), natural components can be broadly classified into two categories: direct gene-encoded components, such as sRNA and small peptides, and indirect gene-encoded components, including secondary metabolites and carbohydrates. Each of them plays a crucial role in biological systems and has distinct applications in medicine and biotechnology.9,10 For example, sRNA and small peptide-based therapeutics have demonstrated significant therapeutic potential in drug discovery. sRNA drugs, such as antisense oligonucleotides11 and small interfering RNAs,12 have revolutionized precision medicine by enabling targeted gene regulation. Additionally, the discovery that plant-derived microRNAs (miRNAs) can be absorbed by mammalian tissues and modulate gene expression has opened new avenues for cross-kingdom regulation,13,14 presenting novel strategies for treating genetic disorders and cancers. Similarly, small-peptide drugs, with their remarkable bioactivity and low toxicity, have achieved clinical success by managing conditions such as diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.15,16Figure 1
Characterization of natural components based on the central dogma

Recognizing the significance of natural components, numerous databases have been developed to compile and annotate the components.14,17,18,19 Based on currently identified natural compounds, scientists have developed several natural product databases (Table S1), such as COCONUT 2.0,17 which contains nearly 0.7 million natural components. However, these databases exclusively focus on secondary metabolites and have notable limitations in both classification scope and functional utility. Their structure-based classification overlooks other key gene-encoded natural components, such as sRNAs, peptides, and carbohydrates, leading to an incomplete representation of components. Although a few specialized databases exist for small peptides, sRNA, and carbohydrates (Tables S2–S4), such as peptideAtlas,20 the Bencao sRNA Atlas,14 and GlyTouCan,21 they remain fragmented and do not offer a unified platform for systematically analyzing the full spectrum of natural components. Hence, it could be concluded that existing databases typically focus on a single type of natural component, limiting a comprehensive understanding of the full biochemical landscape within an organism. In addition, despite the vast number of bioactive components derived from traditional medicinal plants, databases specifically dedicated to medicinal species remain scarce, posing challenges for researchers seeking to explore the therapeutic potential of these natural components.

To address these gaps, there is an urgent need for a comprehensive database that integrates diverse natural components within a single framework, enabling systematic investigations of the molecular diversity present in specific species. This need is particularly pronounced for medicinal plants, which are rich sources of bioactive components widely utilized in traditional and modern medicine. The eight globally recognized pharmacopoeias (Brazilian, Egyptian, European, Indian, Japanese, Korean, the Pharmacopoeia of the People’s Republic of China, and the US Pharmacopoeia’s Herbal Medicines Compendium),22 which catalog medicinal plants with well-documented therapeutic properties, provide a valuable foundation for such an endeavor. Therefore, it is imperative to establish a systematic and comprehensive database to support extensive research on medicinal species and enhance drug discovery efforts.

Recent advancements in AI and multi-omics technologies have revolutionized the field of natural components research.23,24 High-throughput genome sequencing, metabolomics, and computational annotation methods now enable large-scale identification and characterization of natural components with unprecedented accuracy and efficiency.25,26 Building on this progress, we have developed the Global Pharmacopoeia Genome Database (GPGD),22 the Traditional Chinese Medicine Plant Genome Database (TCMPG),27 and the 1K Medicinal Plant Genome Database (1K-MPGD),28 laying the groundwork for genomic-level investigations of natural components.

Expanding upon this foundation, we established the Gene-encoded Natural Diverse Compound Repository (GNDC; https://cbcb.cdutcm.edu.cn/gndc/), the first open-access comprehensive database dedicated to gene-encoded natural components. The GNDC integrates annotated data from nuclear and organellar genomes of species listed in eight global pharmacopoeias and multiple public resources. GNDC is a vast repository of over 234 million natural components systematically categorized into four specialized sub-databases: HerbalMDB for secondary metabolites, HerbalPDB for small peptides, HerbalRDB for sRNA, and HerbalCDB for carbohydrates. Beyond being a comprehensive data repository, GNDC incorporates advanced analytical tools that will enable researchers to investigate genetic encoding mechanisms, uncover the diversity of natural compounds, and assess their potential pharmaceutical applications.

sec.title: Secondary metabolites
sec.p: HerbalMDB consolidates fundamental information on secondary metabolites from multiple sources (Table S1) and eight global pharmacopoeias. Additionally, AI-driven approaches have been employed to supplement and refine the dataset, enhancing data completeness and accuracy. To further improve data utility, a structured annotation pipeline was implemented for each acquired secondary metabolite (Figure S2), and the code for this pipeline is openly available at GitHub (https://github.com/GreatChenLab/GNDC/tree/main/SMDB) for transparency and reproducibility.

sec.title: Analyzing the biosynthetic precursors of secondary metabolites
sec.p: BioNavi-NP was used to analyze the synthetic pathways of secondary metabolites.29 The methodological details of BioNavi-NP are provided in the supplemental information. Through this analysis, we identified the biosynthetic precursors of secondary metabolites, which also exhibit bioactivity, as indicated in our previous work.30

sec.title: Similarity calculation of secondary metabolites
sec.p: To ensure data consistency, duplicate entries were removed based on simplified molecular input line entry system (SMILES) representations, followed by normalization using RDKit (v.2017.09.3). Morgan fingerprints were then generated via RDKit (v.2017.09.3), and structural similarities among secondary metabolites were assessed using the Tanimoto coefficient. A detailed explanation of the similarity calculation process is provided in the supplemental information.

sec.title: Classification of secondary metabolites
sec.p: Secondary metabolites were classified based on their biosynthetic origins and structural motifs using NPClassifier.31 The computational principles underlying NPClassifier are described in the supplemental information. Through this classification framework, each secondary metabolite was categorized into three hierarchical levels31 (pathways, superclasses, and classes), which facilitates systematic categorization.

sec.title: Prediction of ADMET properties of secondary metabolites
sec.p: The absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) properties of secondary metabolites were predicted using ADMET-AI.32 The methodological detail of ADMET-AI is elaborated in detail in supplemental information. This approach enabled the assessment of key pharmacokinetics and safety-related properties, including ADMET, offering valuable insights into the drug-like potential of secondary metabolites.

sec.title: Perturbation profiles of secondary metabolites
sec.p: The in-house-developed DeepICER framework was employed to evaluate the impact of secondary metabolites on cellular gene expression perturbations (supplemental information). By using DeepICER, we predicted the signature gene expression profiles perturbed by secondary metabolites, providing insights into their potential regulatory roles in biological systems.

sec.title: Small peptides
sec.p: Genomes and associated information for medicinal plants were collected from 1K-MPGD (http://www.herbgenome.com), TCMPG (https://cbcb.cdutcm.edu.cn/TCMPG/), and GPGD (http://www.gpgenome.com/). Based on these data, small peptide annotation and functional analysis were performed in medicinal plants. The detailed pipeline is shown in Figure S3, and the code is available at GitHub (https://github.com/GreatChenLab/GNDC/tree/main/PDB).

sec.title: Annotation of small peptides
sec.p: Small peptides were predicted through an integrative strategy combining genome-based ab initio prediction, transcriptome data analysis, and mass spectrometry validation. The genome-wide prediction of small peptides was performed using a six-frame translation approach implemented in EMBOSS (http://emboss.open-bio.org) and ORFIPY (https://github.com/urmi-21/orfipy), generating all possible protein-coding sequences extending from termination codons. Filtering criteria were applied to retain sequences ranging from 5 to 75 amino acids in length. The CD-HIT algorithm with optimized parameters (- c 0.5, - n 3, - l 4) was used to remove redundancy from identified small peptides. To complement genome-based predictions, transcriptome data from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra) were aligned to their corresponding reference genomes using HISAT2 (https://daehwankimlab.github.io/hisat2/). Reconstructed transcripts were processed with StringTie (https://github.com/gpertea/stringtie), and coding sequences were identified using TransDecoder (https://github.com/TransDecoder/TransDecoder). The mmseq2 (https://github.com/soedinglab/MMseqs2, release 17-b804f) was used to compare transcriptome-annotated proteins with genome-predicted small peptides, generating a small peptide dataset supported by transcriptome data. For further validation, mass spectrometry data were incorporated to enhance the confidence of predicted small peptides. Experimentally derived small peptide sequences were compared against the genome- and transcriptome-predicted datasets using BLASTp (https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/BlastAlign.cgi), and peptides with significant sequence matches were retained as high-confidence candidates.

sec.title: Functional annotation of small peptides
sec.p: The functional characterization of small peptides was performed through comparative analyses against established protein function and pathway databases. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway annotations were assigned using HMMSCAN (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/Tools/hmmer/search/hmmscan), enabling the identification of metabolic and signaling pathways associated with these small peptides. Functional classification was further refined through sequence homology searches against the UniProt database using BLASTp, providing insights into potential biological roles and molecular interactions. To evaluate the physicochemical properties of small peptides, including pH, optical rotation, and isoelectric point, predictions were conducted using the ProtParam module within Bio.SeqUtils (https://biopython.org/docs/1.75/api/Bio.SeqUtils.html). In addition to general physicochemical characterization, specialized bioactivity predictions were performed to assess potential therapeutic applications. Antimicrobial activity was predicted using iAMPCN (https://github.com/joy50706/iAMPCN) with default parameters, while anti-inflammatory properties were assessed using PepNet.33 The blood-brain barrier permeability of small peptides was evaluated using DeepB3P (https://github.com/GreatChenLab/DeepB3P).34

sec.title: sRNA
sec.p: HerbalRDB integrates information on sRNAs of herbal medicines. The annotation processes are illustrated in Figure S4, and the code has been uploaded to GitHub (https://github.com/GreatChenLab/GNDC/tree/main/RDB).

sec.title: Annotation method of sRNA
sec.p: To identify genomic regions corresponding to non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families, we employed the Rfam database (v.14.10) alongside INFERNAL software (v.1.1.4) for ncRNA prediction. High-confidence predictions were further refined to extract small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) and miRNAs. The parameters used for Rfam were “-cut_ga -rfam -nohmmonly -fmt 2,” while INFERNAL was executed with “cmscan -cut_ga -nohmmonly -cpu 16 --tblout out.tblout -fmt 2 -clanin Rfam.clanin -rfam Rfam.cm genome.fa.” For tRNA sequence characterization, tRNAscan-SE (v.2.0.12) was employed with the parameters “-E -j tRNA.gff -o tRNA.result -f tRNA.struct.” Additionally, rRNA prediction was conducted using rRNAmmer (v.1.2) with the parameters “-S euk -m tsu, lsu, ssu.” The seqkit software was used to identify and eliminate duplicate sRNA entries that were output in the same species. This process was executed with the parameter set to “rmdup -s.”

sec.title: Functional annotation of miRNA
sec.p: A bioinformatics analysis pipeline was employed to predict miRNAs and their target genes. First, miRNA sequencing (miRNA-seq) datasets were collected from NCBI and formatted. The tBtools_JRE1.6.jar biocjava.sRNA.Tools.sRNAseqAdaperRemover software was used to remove splice sequences from the sequencing data, followed by merging and de-redundancy of reads with identical sequences using the parameter “--minLen 17.”

Based on the genome annotations provided in the GFF file, gffread (v.0.12.7) was utilized to extract gene sequences from the genome. To further validate the reliability of the genome-predicted precursor miRNAs, the mmseq2 software (release 17-b804f) (https://github.com/soedinglab/MMseqs2) was used to blast them with miRNA-seq resolved precursor miRNAs. The parameters was “--search-type 3 --threads 16'”. In addition, the best-matched mature miRNAs are also evidential support for genomic prediction of precursor miRNAs. RNAhybrid (v.2.1.2) was used to analyze the complementary pairing patterns between miRNA sequences and target mRNA sequences to identify potential binding sites. The secondary structure of target genes was evaluated, and binding stability was assessed by calculating the free energy of miRNA target interactions. High-confidence targets with enhanced binding stability and biological relevance were prioritized for further analysis.

To annotate the function of miRNA target genes, different resources were used based on gene type. For coding RNA targets, functional annotations and gene-specific information were retrieved from the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (HGNC) database (https://www.genenames.org/), along with Gene Ontology (GO) annotations. For non-coding RNA targets, detailed genomic context and regulatory features were accessed via the NCBI database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/).

sec.title: Carbohydrates
sec.p: A total of 244,844 carbohydrate entries were compiled from GlyTouCan (https://glycosmos.org/download). These entries include information such as International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (IUPAC) names, ChEBI entries, PubChem chemical identifiers (CIDs), WURCS notations, motif names, and taxonomy details. To categorize species information, the NCBI database was utilized to classify GlyTouCan-derived carbohydrates into animals, insects, plants, and microorganisms. After filtering, 235,331 carbohydrate entries derived from plants, insects, and microorganisms were retained for further analysis. To enhance chemical annotation, structural descriptors such as SMILES, InChIKey, molecular formulas, molecular weights, and synonyms were retrieved using PubChemPy (v.1.0.4) based on the PubChem CIDs obtained from GlyTouCan. Besides, 8,571 carbohydrate entries from plants and fungi were manually collected from the Carbohydrate Structure Database (CSDB; https://csdb.glycoscience.ru/database/), including SMILES, molecular formulas, molecular weights, and species information. Corresponding InChIKeys, PubChem CIDs, and synonyms for these carbohydrates were further retrieved via PubChemPy (v.1.0.4) based on the SMILES from CSDB. In addition, 23,324 carbohydrate molecules previously annotated in secondary metabolites section were also incorporated.

To ensure data consistency, duplicate carbohydrate entries were identified and removed by comparing their SMILES and taxonomy information. Glycan structures were generated using GlycoWork (v.1.5.0) and GlycoDraw based on Glycan IUPAC names, ensuring compliance with the Symbol Nomenclature for Glycans (SNFG) guidelines. The pipeline for carbohydrate data processing and curation is provided in Figure S5, and the code for this pipeline is openly available at GitHub (https://github.com/GreatChenLab/GNDC/tree/main/CDB).

sec.title: Website development
sec.p: The GNDC platform (https://cbcb.cdutcm.edu.cn/gndc/) is developed using the Django framework, leveraging SQLite as its database backend and deployed on a Linux server. Django’s object-relational mapping is utilized to facilitate secure and efficient data management. The front end is built with HTML5 and Bootstrap, with interactive functionalities implemented via JavaScript and jQuery. To optimize performance, Redis is employed for caching. Additionally, the platform incorporates robust security measures, including HTTPS enforcement, data encryption, and cross-site request forgery protection, ensuring the integrity and confidentiality of biological data.

sec.title: Content of GNDC
sec.p:
In this release, GNDC encompasses more than 234 million of natural diverse components derived from thousands of organisms (Table S5), making it the world’s first gene-encoded diverse natural components repository. Its uniqueness lies in the large scale of data and the multidimensional annotation of information (Figure 2A). GNDC currently includes four distinct databases (HerbalMDB, HerbalPDB, HerbalRDB, and HerbalCDB), which were designed to organize and provide information on secondary metabolites, small peptides, sRNAs, and carbohydrates, respectively.Figure 2
Schematic overview of the GNDC content
(A) Function diagram of the sub-databases in GNDC, highlighting key data categories and functional modules for data retrieval and analysis.
(B) Phylogenetic tree of species cataloged in eight global pharmacopoeias. The innermost circle denotes the corresponding species and their taxonomic classifications as defined by the NCBI Taxonomy database. Moving outward, the next four concentric circles sequentially illustrate the number of metabolites, small peptides, sRNAs and carbohydrates identified in each species. FA, fatty acid; PK, polyketide; S&P, shikimate-phenylpropanoid; AK, alkaloid; Terp, terpenoid.

HerbalMDB houses over 2,321,763 secondary metabolites spanning five biosynthetic pathways. It also includes functional modules such as biosynthetic precursor analysis, structural similarity analysis, compound classification, ADMET property assessment, and gene expression profile prediction, along with the information on secondary metabolites obtained from these analyses. HerbalPDB contains over 229,772,278 small peptides annotated based on genomic, transcriptomic, and peptidomic data. Additionally, the database provides physicochemical properties as well as information on bioactivity profiles, including antimicrobial activity, blood-brain barrier permeability, and anti-inflammatory effects. HerbalRDB documents 2,382,463 sRNAs, including miRNAs, tRNAs, rRNAs, and snRNAs. It also incorporates functional modules such as species information, GC content analysis, and miRNA target gene prediction, along with the sRNA data obtained from these analyses. HerbalCDB contains a total of 264,564 carbohydrates covering polysaccharides, oligosaccharides, and monosaccharides together with information on species, SNFG, and other relevant annotations.

Using species cataloged in the eight global pharmacopoeias as examples, we annotated secondary metabolites, small peptides, sRNAs, and carbohydrates from these species. Their distributions were visualized by using the phylogenetic tree constructed based on the NCBI Taxonomy database (Figure 2B). This result provides valuable insights into the taxonomic diversity of these natural diverse components, highlighting their prevalence across different lineages.

sec.title: Advantages of GNDC over existing databases
sec.p:
To demonstrate the merits of GNDC, we conducted comparative analyses with representative databases. The results highlight the significant advantages of HerbalMDB, HerbalPDB, and HerbalRDB in terms of data scale, annotation depth, and functional insights. HerbalMDB surpasses representative secondary metabolite databases (Table S2) in both data scale and annotation depth (Figure 3A). Compared to the representative databases COCONUT and SuperNatural, GNDC has added 1,626,630 and 1,118,227 unique secondary metabolites, representing an increase of 234% and 92.91%, respectively. Notably, GNDC includes 87,679 newly added secondary metabolites that have not been reported in any of the referenced databases, accounting for 3.78% of the total. Beyond data scale and fundamental annotations such as biogenetic origin, classification, 2D structure, ADMET properties, computed descriptors, and structural similarity, HerbalMDB uniquely incorporates expression profile perturbed by metabolites, enhancing its functional utility. HerbalPDB outperforms existing small-peptide databases (Table S3) in data size (Figure 3B), and nearly 98% of the total number of peptides are new entries. In addition to GO and KEGG pathway associations, HerbalPDB uniquely incorporates key functional attributes, including physicochemical traits, antimicrobial properties, blood-brain barrier penetration potential, and anti-inflammatory effects. HerbalRDB excels existing sRNA databases (Table S4) not only in data scale but also in comprehensiveness. Compared with the most comprehensive herbal sRNA database, the Bencao sRNA Atlas (Table S4), 1,636,078 new entries have been added, accounting for 219.20% of the total number of sRNAs. HerbalRDB also stands out for its genomic reliability, broad species coverage, comprehensive sRNA classification, systematic miRNA-seq integration, and well-annotated targets (Figure 3C).Figure 3
Comparison of GNDC and other databases in terms of data scale and information
Shown are HerbalMDB (A), HerbalPDB (B), and HerbalRDB (C), illustrating a comparative analysis of data scale (left)and a comparison of depth of annotations (right).

sec.title: Functional description of each section of the database
HerbalMDB
sec.p:
HerbalMDB (https://cbcb.cdutcm.edu.cn/smdb) allows users to browse, query, and analyze secondary metabolites through the options in the navigation bar (Figure 4A).Figure 4
Screenshots of the web interfaces of HerbalMDB
(A) Overview of the functional modules in HerbalMDB.
(B) The Browse module.
(C) The Query module.
(D) Detailed page for deposited metabolites.
(E) Integrated tools in HerbalMDB.

In the data browsing module of HerbalMDB, the top five distributions of pathway, superclass, and class among secondary metabolites are visually presented. Each entry is displayed in a list format, including key details such as structure, species, pathway, superclass, and class. Users can click on the chemical formula to access comprehensive information about the selected secondary metabolite (Figure 4B). HerbalMDB features a versatile query module that enables users to construct customized searches by using Boolean operators (Figure 4C). The module supports a range of search criteria, including structural information (structure drawing and SMILES), physicochemical properties (molecular weight, LogP, HBA, HBD, TPSA, Lipinski compliance, stereo centers, and QED weighted), and secondary metabolite identifiers (metabolite name, IUPAC name, molecular formula, and standard InChI key). Additionally, users can refine searches based on species and classification (class, superclass, and pathway). After defining the search criteria, users can execute the query by clicking the search button in the top right corner of the interface (Figure 4C). The result page displays a list of matching secondary metabolites, where users can click on a metabolite name or its corresponding icon to access a detailed information page. This page includes essential details such as the metabolite’s basic properties, the five most structurally similar metabolites, and its natural sources. Additionally, it provides information on the metabolite’s ADMET profile, covering absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity predictions as well as its gene expression patterns influenced by the metabolite (Figure 4D).

To enhance the usability and functional depth of HerbalMDB, we have integrated several secondary metabolite analysis tools, including NPClassifier, ADMET-AI, and DeepICER (Figure 4E). By incorporating these analytical tools, HerbalMDB provides a streamlined platform for structural annotation, functional evaluation, and bioactivity prediction, supporting both exploratory research and drug discovery.

sec.title: HerbalPDB
sec.p:
HerbalPDB catalogs small peptides and is available at https://cbcb.cdutcm.edu.cn/pep_db/. Its primary functional modules include browse and query (Figure 5A). In the browsing module, each small peptide entry is displayed with details including its ID, species name, sequence information, and functional annotations from KEGG and UniProt. Each peptide’s support evidence is indicated as follows: G for de novo genome analysis, R for RNA sequencing, and P for peptidomics (Figure 5B). The query builder allows for advanced searches based on species name, KEGG ID, or UniProt ID (Figure 5C). Every GO term and KEGG ID within the database is hyperlinked to its official webpage, providing access to detailed functional information (Figure 5D). The small peptide ID links lead to its basic information, including physicochemical properties such as pH, optical rotation, and isoelectric point, along with annotations for antimicrobial peptides, anti-inflammatory peptides, and blood-brain barrier permeability (Figure 5E).Figure 5

sec.title: HerbalRDB
sec.p: HerbalRDB (https://cbcb.cdutcm.edu.cn/small_rna/) is a platform designed to consolidate and analyze multidimensional information on sRNAs derived from traditional herbal medicines. It functions as a centralized hub for researchers to explore the functional roles of sRNAs through advanced data retrieval, visualization, and analysis modules.

The dashboard offers smooth navigation between core modules (Data Repository, Browse, and Query Builder) via a navigation bar (Figure 6A). Each sRNA entry is annotated with a unique sRNA ID, species origin, RNA type (miRNA, tRNA, rRNA, or snRNA), sequence, GC content, target genes for miRNAs, and evidence information (G for genomic and R for transcriptome) (Figure 6B). Clicking on an sRNA ID opens a detailed view displaying the sequence, secondary structure visualization, and target gene lists (Figure 6C). For coding RNAs in the miRNA target gene list, users can access the HGNC database and retrieve GO annotations via embedded hyperlinks. For non-coding RNAs, hyperlinks direct users to the NCBI database, which provides extensive genomic details and annotations (Figure 6D).Figure 6

The Query Builder functionality allows users to input a species name with fuzzy matching capabilities for flexible querying. Users can also input target gene ID or sequence to query for targets of interest, both of which also support fuzzy matching for flexible querying (Figure 6E).

sec.title: HerbalCDB
sec.p:
HerbalCDB, available at https://cbcb.cdutcm.edu.cn/CarbohydrateDB/, is a carbohydrate database that allows users to browse and search for carbohydrates (Figure 7A). In HerbalCDB, users can browse various carbohydrates with key details, including IUPAC name, SMILES, molecular weight, molecular formula, InChIKey, and structural representations (Figure 7B). HerbalCDB features an efficient query function that supports multiple search modules, including carbohydrate ID, IUPAC name, CID, molecular formula, InChIKey, and taxonomy, enabling rapid identification of target glycans (Figure 7C). Additionally, HerbalCDB also incorporates a range of analytical tools and resources, including Glycowork, VirtualGlycome, RINGS, ISOGlyP, GRITS toolbox, and NMRDB (Figure 7D).Figure 7

sec.title: Profiling of natural diverse components using GNDC
sec.p: Panax ginseng, a renowned medicinal plant of the Araliaceae family, is rich in diverse bioactive components and exhibits extensive pharmacological activities against various diseases.35,36 To demonstrate the power and usefulness of GNDC, we conducted a case study on P. ginseng, focusing on its secondary metabolites, small peptides, sRNA, and carbohydrates.

In terms of secondary metabolites, HerbalMDB comprises 3,265 ginseng-related secondary metabolites, including 2,278 newly annotated compounds analyzed using BioNavi-NP. A statistical classification of both the original and newly annotated secondary metabolites revealed that most belong to key categories such as terpenoids, fatty acids, shikimates, and phenylpropanoids. Furthermore, clustering analysis using Morgan fingerprints and the t-SNE algorithm demonstrated that the original and newly identified metabolites occupy distinct regions within the clustering space (Figure 8A). This suggests that the expanded dataset significantly broadens the explored chemical landscape, enhancing the diversity and potential applications of ginseng-derived metabolites.Figure 8
Multi-perspective visualization of natural components in P. ginseng
(A) The number of secondary metabolites increased across all five pathway terms. Compared to the original secondary metabolites, the newly obtained ones have significantly expanded the chemical space.
(B) Top: GO annotation of 4,488 small peptides from P. ginseng. Bottom: number of annotated small peptides in different databases for the 4,488 small peptides, along with their KEGG annotation.
(C) Comparison of ginseng-derived sRNA quantities and functional annotations of miRNA target genes in HerbalRDB and the original database.
(D) Number and type of carbohydrates of P. ginseng in HerbalCDB.

Leveraging the whole genome data of P. ginseng, we annotated a total of 800,571 small peptides. To enhance the reliability of this dataset, we integrated transcriptome and peptidome data, ultimately identifying 4,488 small peptides that were consistently supported across all three data sources (Table S6). Among them, 190 and 139 small peptides were further validated through the UniProt and KEGG databases, respectively. Functional analysis of the 4,488 small peptides revealed their involvement in key biological processes. In the GO classification, they were predominantly associated with carbohydrate metabolic process and proteolysis. Regarding cellular component classification, they were primarily linked to cytosol, cytoplasm, and membrane. At the molecular function level, these small peptides exhibited ATP-binding, metal ion binding, and ATP hydrolysis activity. Additionally, KEGG pathway annotation indicated that these small peptides play crucial roles in translation, energy metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and amino acid metabolism (Figure 8B).

A total of 22,307 sRNAs were obtained from P. ginseng, comprising 8,939 miRNAs, 1,447 tRNAs, 9,903 snRNAs, and 2,018 rRNAs and were systematically curated within HerbalRDB, significantly expanding the original database, which encompassed only 304 sRNAs (Figure 8C). To further elucidate their biological significance, taking the derived miRNAs as an example, we investigate their regulatory roles in cross-kingdom interactions. These ginseng-derived miRNAs are notably involved in key metabolic processes and human diseases, including immune disorders, cancers, and metabolic syndromes. HerbalRDB significantly enriches the functional landscape of ginseng miRNAs by integrating additional pathway annotations related to cellular processes, environmental information processing, genetic information processing, and organismal systems, thereby expanding their potential applications in biomedical research and therapeutic development.

HerbalCDB currently deposited carbohydrates from P. ginseng, including monosaccharides, disaccharides, trisaccharides, octasaccharides, nonasaccharides, and polysaccharides. To facilitate comprehensive analysis, each carbohydrate is accompanied by detailed information such as chemical formula, molecular weight, IUPAC name, SMILES, InChIKeys, and structural details (Figure 8D). This extensive information offers valuable insights into the carbohydrate composition of P. ginseng, providing a robust foundation for future research on pharmacological potential and therapeutic applications.

To further demonstrate the generalizability of GNDC across taxonomically diverse species, we conducted an additional case study on Polygala tenuifolia, a medicinal plant with distinct phylogenetic characteristics. A total of 1,409 secondary metabolites were identified in P. tenuifolia, among which 1,068 were newly discovered and not previously reported in existing databases. These metabolites were primarily classified into major categories, including shikimates and phenylpropanoids, polyketides, and terpenoids (Figure S6A). Clustering analysis based on their chemical structures revealed that the newly identified compounds formed distinct clusters, suggesting unique chemical properties and potential novel biological activities (Figure S6A).

A total of 687,975 small peptides were identified from P. tenuifolia. Among them, 22,336 and 8,119 small peptides were confirmed through the UniProt and KEGG databases, respectively. In GO classification, these peptides showed significant enrichment in biological processes related to DNA integration, phosphorylation, and proteolysis. Regarding cellular components, they were predominantly localized to membrane, nucleus, and cytoplasm. At the molecular functional level, the peptides demonstrated binding activities, including ATP binding, nucleic acid binding, and metal ion binding. Furthermore, KEGG pathway analysis revealed their critical involvement in carbohydrate metabolism, protein folding/sorting/degradation processes, and signal transduction pathways (Figure S6B).

A total of 9,827 sRNAs were obtained from P. tenuifolia, comprising 206 miRNAs, 739 tRNAs, 1,482 snRNAs, and 7,400 rRNAs, and were systematically curated within HerbalRDB, addressing the gap in existing databases by providing comprehensive annotation of sRNAs in P. tenuifolia (Figure S6C).

Twenty-six distinct carbohydrate compounds were isolated from P. tenuifolia, comprising disaccharides, trisaccharides, tetrasaccharides, and pentasaccharides. Each compound is accompanied by detailed chemical information such as IUPAC names, molecular formula, SMILES notation, molecular weight, InChIKeys, and structural illustrations (Figure S6D).

This case study, alongside that of P. ginseng, underscores GNDC’s robust performance in profiling natural components across species, highlighting its broad applicability for natural product research in both traditional and non-model organisms.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Natural components have long been a cornerstone of pharmaceutical development, providing a vast array of bioactive compounds that serve as the foundation for many modern drugs. However, the study and application of natural products have been hindered by challenges such as their structural complexity, biosynthetic diversity, and the fragmented nature of existing databases.37,38 Traditional natural product databases primarily classify compounds based on chemical structures, lacking an integrative framework that links genomic information with natural diversity.

To address these limitations, by leveraging artificial intelligence and multi-omics analytical techniques, we developed a unified platform, GNDC, that integrates over 234 million natural components, including secondary metabolites, small peptides, sRNAs, and carbohydrates. Unlike existing databases, which are categorized primarily by chemical structure or species origin, GNDC systematically classifies and annotates natural components based on the central dogma of molecular biology. This novel gene-encoding framework provides a more comprehensive and functionally relevant perspective by bridging the gap between genomic information and natural compound diversity. Compounds are categorized according to their genomic origin—either directly gene encoded (e.g., sRNAs, peptides) or indirectly encoded via gene-regulated enzymatic pathways (e.g., secondary metabolites). This genomic linkage enables integration with transcriptomic data and biosynthetic gene clusters, facilitating deeper insight into molecular biosynthesis and regulation.

From an evolutionary biology perspective, directly encoded molecules often evolve through gene-level changes such as duplication or horizontal gene transfer, whereas secondary metabolites originate from biosynthetic gene clusters that evolve in a modular fashion. This distinction reflects adaptive strategies organisms use to interact with their environment. Regarding metabolic regulation, directly encoded molecules are typically controlled at the transcriptional or translational level, while indirectly encoded metabolites involve complex regulatory networks spanning multiple genes and pathways. Hence, this gene-encoded framework is particularly advantageous in the study and rational application of herbal medicines, where mixtures of diverse bioactive compounds act synergistically. Traditional structure-based methods often struggle to represent such complexity. In contrast, the gene-based classification aligns chemical diversity with biological function, supporting a more holistic, systems-level understanding of natural products across modern and traditional medicine contexts.

Despite the significant advancements brought by GNDC, we still face various challenges that require innovative solutions. Although AI tools have greatly enhanced data annotation and functional inference in GNDC, their predictions are still subject to uncertainties and potential biases, especially when applied to novel or underrepresented compound types. These tools rely on training datasets that may not fully capture the structural diversity of natural products, and in some cases, predicted properties or targets require further experimental validation. In another aspect, secondary metabolites remain a largely untapped resource due to their biosynthesis often being controlled by cryptic gene clusters. Unraveling these pathways requires genome mining and synthetic biology approaches to fully explore their chemical diversity and pharmaceutical potential. In parallel, small peptides present unique difficulties, as many bioactive small peptides originate from non-canonical reading frames and undergo extensive post-translational modifications. To address this, integrating peptidomics with mass spectrometry-based validation is crucial for improving their annotation and functional characterization. In future research, we will gradually increase the support of transcriptome and mass spectrometry data to obtain more high-quality small peptides. Beyond small peptides, sRNAs, particularly regulatory RNAs, offer promising therapeutic avenues. However, while genomic and transcriptomic sequencing has identified vast numbers of these molecules, their biological roles often remain elusive due to the lack of efficient functional validation methods. High-throughput functional assays, coupled with machine learning-based predictive models, will be essential for uncovering their mechanisms of action. Carbohydrates, known for their structural complexity and heterogeneity, present challenges in standardization and annotation. This is also the reason why our database contains limited information on carbohydrates. Advances in glycomics, combined with computational modeling, will be key to refining their characterization and expanding their biomedical and industrial applications. By addressing these challenges through interdisciplinary approaches and advanced analytical techniques, GNDC will continue to drive innovation in natural product research and drug discovery.

In the future, GNDC will continue expanding its database to incorporate a broader range of biologically derived natural components, including those from marine organisms, microorganisms, and rare medicinal species. In addition to expanding its content, GNDC will focus on implementing real-time data updates, ensuring that the latest discoveries in genomics, metabolomics, and structural biology are continuously integrated. Since understanding how genes and enzymes precisely regulate the biosynthesis of these components remains a complex issue, a key priority will be the refinement of biosynthetic pathway reconstructions, leveraging advanced computational models to annotate novel biosynthetic pathways with greater accuracy. By addressing these challenges through interdisciplinary collaboration and cutting-edge analytical techniques, GNDC will drive the transformation of natural component-based drug discovery from an experience-driven approach to a big data-driven paradigm.
